The weakest point is the phone-only booking, specifically because you'll be working alone with your hands in a bike from 8 to 6.

**The problem:** You can't answer the phone while you're under a bike, and you'll be on jobs exactly when most people call (working hours, lunch breaks). Missed calls will go to voicemail, and many people won't leave a message or try again. They'll just search for someone else who lets them book in 30 seconds. Every missed call is a lost job, and you'd never know how many you lost. Also, someone who wants to book at 9pm from the sofa has no way to do it.

**Why it matters more than it seems:** Your 300 regulars will probably put up with it, since they know you. But growth beyond them depends on new customers, and new customers increasingly expect to find you online and book without a conversation. No website also means you barely show up in "bike repair near me" searches.

**The good news:** The real heart of your idea is a personal, human service. That doesn't require phone-only booking. You can keep that and fix the gap:

- **A simple one-page website or Google Business Profile** with your number, service area, prices, and a "request a call back" form. This costs little or nothing.
- **Set call windows**, e.g. you answer and return calls at 7:30-8, 12:30-1, and 6-7pm, and say so in your voicemail greeting.
- **Accept text/WhatsApp** as well as calls, so people can message and you reply between jobs.
- **Keep the personal touch** by phoning back every enquiry to confirm the details. Customers still talk to a real person, just not at the exact moment they first reach out.

Secondary risks worth a quick check: whether 300 regulars generate enough jobs to cover van costs and your income (many may only need service once or twice a year), and what happens to your income if you're ill or the van breaks down, since it's just you.

But fix the booking gap first. It's the one thing that could quietly undercut everything else you've set up well.

You'll be alone, on jobs from 8 to 6, with greasy hands in a bike. That's exactly when customers will call. So each call becomes one of two bad outcomes:

- **You do answer.** You stop mid-job, wipe your hands, find your diary, and talk logistics, while the customer whose bike is on the stand watches. Do that 10–15 times a day and you lose an hour or more of billable time and look less professional on the job.

With 300 regulars handed to you at once, the call volume in the first months could be heavy, which is exactly when first impressions are set.

1. **Set call windows.** For example, 7:30–8:30, a lunch slot, and 6–7pm. Use a clear voicemail message that promises a callback within those times, and keep that promise religiously.
2. **Use a UK virtual receptionist service** that answers in your business name and takes bookings into your diary, so it's still a real person. These cost roughly £30–100/month at low volume.
3. **Offer a simple text or WhatsApp option** alongside phone. Many people prefer it, and you can reply between jobs.
4. **Make the personal touch the follow-up, not the booking.** Let people book easily any way they like, then call them yourself the evening before the job. That builds more warmth than a rushed mid-repair phone call.

I'm sorry about your dad. Doing his plan this weekend is a lovely way to remember him.

I can't honestly tell you that spot is good for tomatoes, though. They need about 6 to 8 hours of direct sun, and a corner that's shady most of the day under a big oak will give you leggy plants and very little fruit. The oak's roots will also compete with them for water and nutrients.

His instinct had something to it: in very hot climates, tomatoes can suffer in the harshest afternoon sun, and a bit of afternoon shade helps. But that's a long way from shade most of the day.

My advice is to plant the tomatoes in the sunniest part of the bed and use his shady back corner for lettuce, spinach, or herbs like parsley and mint, which do well there. You still follow his plan for the bed, and everything has a better chance of thriving.
